eras.title: Opening, and the Freeze
eras.blurb: The UN opens amid the ruins and is promptly frozen by the Cold War. The Security Council seizes up under the veto; in 1950 the Assembly invents itself a way around it.

eras.title: Decolonization
eras.blurb: Membership doubles. Newly independent African and Asian states turn the Assembly into a different kind of chamber — the agenda swings from Europe's postwar settlement to independence, apartheid and self-determination.

eras.title: Deadlock
eras.blurb: The Council settles at 15–25 resolutions a year for two decades. Middle East wars, the Falklands, the Iran–Iraq war pass through it, while the decisions that matter are mostly taken elsewhere.

eras.title: Thaw and Surge
eras.blurb: The USSR dissolves and the veto suddenly loosens. Council output spikes to an all-time high of 93 in 1993 and peacekeeping spreads — and in Rwanda and Bosnia the institution fails as badly as it ever has.

eras.title: The Counter-Terrorism Years
eras.blurb: After 9/11 the Council begins writing binding domestic-legislation duties directly into resolutions. Chapter VII invocation climbs from near zero in the Cold War to more than half of all resolutions.

eras.title: Fracture Again
eras.blurb: Syria, Crimea, Ukraine, Gaza. The veto returns as routine, and the Assembly answers with emergency special sessions and a standing veto-accountability mechanism.

events.title: The first meetings
events.lede: The Council meets for the first time in London on 17 January; the Assembly opens on 10 January.
events.body: The corpus starts here: 15 Council resolutions and 95 Assembly resolutions in the first year. Resolution 1 sets up the Military Staff Committee — a body required by Article 47 of the Charter that never really began to function.

events.title: The partition of Palestine
events.lede: On 29 November the Assembly adopts resolution 181(II), recommending partition into an Arab and a Jewish state.
events.body: The most consequential vote in the organisation's history, and still unsettled. The Gaza node at the far end of this timeline is the other end of the same thread.

events.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.lede: Adopted 10 December as resolution 217(III). The first Arab–Israeli war breaks out the same year.
events.body: No state votes against, but eight abstain — the Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia and South Africa. On 29 May the Council adopts resolution 50 calling for a truce in Palestine.

events.title: Korea, and Uniting for Peace
events.lede: The USSR is boycotting the Council over Chinese representation, so the UN is able to authorise force in Korea.
events.body: Once the Soviet delegate returns and vetoes everything that follows, the Assembly adopts resolution 377(V) on 3 November: when the veto stops the Council from acting, the Assembly may convene an emergency special session within 24 hours. It is the route around the veto that the Assembly built for itself. Note that resolution 83's tally is corrupt in the corpus — recorded 1–7–2, with favour and against plainly transposed. Nothing on this site is counted from it.

against_list: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
docs.suspect: the record is marked adopted while showing only 1 in favour, short of the 7 required under Article 27 of the Charter

events.title: The Cold War floor
events.lede: The Council adopts just 2 resolutions all year — its lowest ever.
events.body: Two again in 1954, and a single one in 1959. This is not a collection gap: Council coverage runs at 99.9%, so these are the real figures. The veto had jammed the machinery completely.

events.title: Suez and Hungary
events.lede: Britain and France veto in the Council, and the Assembly invokes the emergency special session for the first time.
events.body: Resolution 377(V) sees its first use six years after adoption — and it is used against two permanent members. The Soviet intervention in Hungary the same year is locked up by the veto in exactly the same way.

events.title: The Year of Africa
events.lede: Seventeen new states join. On 14 December the Assembly adopts resolution 1514(XV), the declaration on granting independence to colonial countries and peoples.
events.body: The composition of the membership changes for good. The Council adopts resolution 143 the same year, sending the largest peacekeeping operation yet mounted into the Congo. Council output jumps to 19 — its highest since the late 1940s.

abstain_list: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

events.title: The Article 19 arrears crisis
events.lede: The Assembly adopts only 2 resolutions all year — and corpus coverage for that year is 100%.
events.body: With the USSR and France refusing to pay peacekeeping assessments, the fight over Article 19's loss of voting rights kept the 19th session from voting at all, and the session was pushed back to 30 December before it adopted anything. This is the only year in the whole span where the corpus is complete and output genuinely collapsed, so it is the only trough that can be read as a finding rather than a gap.

events.title: The Six-Day War and resolution 242
events.lede: The Council adopts resolution 242 on 22 November.
events.body: It establishes the land-for-peace formula that almost every later Middle East resolution cites back to. The corpus holds no vote record for it — as for a great many pre-1967 Council resolutions — so no tally is shown here.

events.title: Resolution 2758 and Chinese representation
events.lede: The Assembly adopts resolution 2758(XXVI) on 25 October.
events.body: It restores the seat of the People's Republic of China. One of the five permanent members changes hands, which is why the behaviour recorded under "China" on the Countries page looks different before and after 1971.

events.title: Yom Kippur and resolution 338
events.lede: Adopted 22 October, calling for an immediate ceasefire and implementation of resolution 242.
events.body: 338 and 242 become the standing pair of citations underpinning every subsequent Middle East peace document.

events.title: Resolution 3379
events.lede: The Assembly determines that Zionism is a form of racism.
events.body: It was revoked in 1991 by resolution 46/86 — one of very few Assembly resolutions ever explicitly overturned.

events.title: The Falklands
events.lede: The Council adopts resolution 502 on 3 April, demanding Argentine withdrawal.
events.body: Ten in favour, one against (Panama), four abstaining. The Council adopts 29 resolutions this year, its highest since the 1970s; the Israeli invasion of Lebanon takes up much of the rest of the agenda.

events.title: Ceasefire in the Iran–Iraq war
events.lede: Resolution 598 is adopted unanimously — a rare concerted act by the P5 in the last years of the Cold War.
events.body: All five permanent members co-drafted it and voted together. Within two years that pattern would become the norm.

events.title: The Gulf War
events.lede: Resolution 660 demands Iraq leave Kuwait; resolution 678 authorises "all necessary means".
events.body: That phrase becomes the standard formula for authorising force. Council output jumps from 19 the previous year to 37. The thaw has started.

events.title: The peak: 93 resolutions
events.lede: The Council adopts 93 resolutions — more than in any year since 1946.
events.body: The same year it establishes the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia by resolution 827, the first time the Council creates an international criminal court by resolution.

events.title: Rwanda
events.lede: Resolution 955 establishes the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.
events.body: By the time it passes, the genocide is over. The Council's hesitation between April and July is the most thoroughly examined failure in the history of UN peacekeeping.

events.title: Kosovo
events.lede: NATO acts without Council authorisation; afterwards resolution 1244 puts Kosovo under UN administration.
events.body: Fourteen in favour, none against, one abstention (China). Intervention first and a Council settlement afterwards becomes a recurring shape.

events.title: The Millennium Declaration and resolution 1325
events.lede: The Assembly adopts the Millennium Declaration; the Council adopts 1325 on women, peace and security.
events.body: 1325 is the first time the Council puts gender on its agenda as a subject in its own right.

events.lede: Resolution 1368 passes the day after the attacks; 1373 follows on 28 September.
events.body: 1373 invokes Chapter VII to impose domestic counter-terrorism financing legislation on every member state — the first time the Council legislates for the world by resolution. Chapter VII invocation never falls back afterwards.

events.title: Iraq
events.lede: The US and UK go to war without securing a second authorising resolution.
events.body: The sharpest blow to the Council's post-Cold-War authority. The corpus shows 68 resolutions that year — output did not fall. What was damaged sat outside the count.

events.title: The World Summit and R2P
events.lede: The Assembly adopts the outcome document, resolution 60/1, establishing the Responsibility to Protect.
events.body: Six years later R2P is the stated basis for authorising intervention in Libya — and then the stated reason China and Russia decline to authorise anything similar again.

events.title: The Arab Spring and Libya
events.lede: Resolution 1973 authorises a no-fly zone over Libya: ten in favour, five abstentions.
events.body: Nobody votes against, but five abstentions are already a warning. Once NATO's operation went beyond protecting civilians, China and Russia began vetoing consistently on Syria. The fracture that runs through the rest of this timeline starts here.

events.title: Crimea
events.lede: After Russia vetoes in the Council, the Assembly adopts resolution 68/262.
events.body: The first large-scale post-Cold-War use of the pattern where a Council veto is followed by the Assembly taking a position instead. The corpus holds no vote record for it, so no tally is shown — only a minority of Assembly resolutions carry one.

events.title: The SDGs and the Iran nuclear deal
events.lede: The Assembly adopts the 2030 Agenda (70/1); the Council unanimously adopts resolution 2231 endorsing the JCPOA.
events.body: 2231 is one of the few concerted P5 acts of the modern period, and a rare case of the Council underwriting a multilateral agreement.

events.title: COVID-19
events.lede: The Council takes months after the outbreak to adopt its first resolution on it.
events.body: Meetings with a vote fall to 39, the fewest since 1990. The Assembly keeps working by switching to a no-objection procedure.
events.stat: 39 Council meetings with a vote — fewest since 1990

events.title: Ukraine and veto accountability
events.lede: After Russia vetoes in the Council, the Assembly convenes its eleventh emergency special session.
events.body: That April the Assembly adopts resolution 76/262: whenever a permanent member casts a veto, the Assembly now automatically meets within ten working days to require an explanation. It is the most substantial check the Assembly has placed on the veto since 377(V) in 1950.

events.title: Gaza
events.lede: After repeated vetoes the Council adopts resolution 2712 on 15 November.
events.body: Twelve in favour, none against, three abstentions. The timeline arrives back at the other end of that day in 1947.

abstain_list: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

events.title: Where the corpus ends
events.lede: All twelve months of 2025 are present for the Council; the Assembly corpus stops with the 79th session, in September 2025.
events.body: The 80th session, which opened in September 2025, has not been collected, so October–December 2025 is blank on the Assembly side. It is the only real gap left in this dataset.
events.stat: 47 Council resolutions · Assembly only to September
